learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the 'big picture' of the economy, tracing the origins of macroeconomics, its unique features, and how it differs from studying individual markets.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Microeconomics studies individual agents like a single consumer or firm. Macroeconomics zooms out to study the economy as a whole, focusing on total output, overall employment, and general price levels.

Before 1929, classical economists believed markets would always fix themselves (full employment). The Great Depression shattered this, as massive unemployment persisted, leading to the birth of modern Macroeconomics.

Keynes is considered the founding father of modern macroeconomics. His 1936 book, 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money', explained that government intervention is needed to pull an economy out of a slump.
An economic system based on private ownership of means of production, where production is for selling in the market to make a profit, and labor is bought and sold at a wage rate.

fun_activity.title: 🔭 The Macro Telescope
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine you are the Finance Minister. Looking through a microscope (Micro), you see one household struggling with their grocery bill. Looking through a telescope (Macro), you see the nation's unemployment rate at 8%. Which tool helps you decide national policy? The telescope!

exam_tips: 📌 Always remember the name and year of John Maynard Keynes' famous book: 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' (1936).
📌 A common board question asks for the differences between Micro and Macroeconomics. Make sure to use examples (Individual income vs. National income).
📌 Know the three main features of a capitalist economy: private ownership, production for the market (profit motive), and wage-labor.
quick_recap: ⭐ Macroeconomics focuses on aggregates like National Income, Total Consumption, and General Price Level.
⭐ The 1929 Great Depression proved that the 'invisible hand' of the market doesn't always guarantee full employment.
⭐ Economic agents include consumers, producers, and the government/central bank (like the RBI).
